problem: Prior target-driven visual navigation (Zhu et al.) targets a specific scene image, requiring the user to have an image taken at the goal location. This is impractical for finding a generic object given only an arbitrary instance image (e.g. from the web).
motivation: Object searching is harder than scene matching because targets can be small and in arbitrary pose. Recognition and navigation had been studied separately, but both now use deep networks, so they can be integrated as an 'active perceiver' where recognition guides the navigation policy.
key_idea: Jointly train a class-agnostic, target-conditioned object recognition module and an A3C-style RL navigation policy that takes the detected object location as input, with a new decaying incremental reward based on the largest detected bounding-box area.
insight: Standard rewards fail on this task: a sparse goal reward (Reward Func. 1) and a plain box-area reward (Reward Func. 2) do not converge and do worse than or equal to random walk on 1 object/1 scene (50% and 0% success vs 60% for random walk). The proposed reward, which only rewards a new largest box, gives 80-100% success and much shorter paths. The exploration-rate ablation shows a trade-off: low entropy weight gives short paths but gets trapped (plate 0% success), high entropy weight succeeds more often but with very long paths.
method: Object recognition module: shared ImageNet-pretrained frozen ResNet-50 (res4f, 1024-d) features for the target object image and the current view; each is projected by an FC layer to 512-d, concatenated and fused, then a classification head (object present?) and a regression head (x, y, w, h box).
Recognition loss: binary cross-entropy for presence plus an L2 box-regression loss active only when the object is present, weighted by λ=0.5.

Policy network: A3C-style deep RL following Zhu et al. with scene-specific layers. The target and observation streams do not share FC weights, because the target image may come from a different domain. The detected object location is encoded as a 5x5 binary map and fed into the fusion layer.
Goal states: the view contains a target box whose size exceeds a threshold, set to the fifth-largest ground-truth box, giving 5 goal states. The robot sees only RGB, with no map or odometry.

Decaying incremental reward: reward equals the box area only when it exceeds the largest area seen so far in the episode, and is discounted by γ over time (Eq. 2). This prevents the robot oscillating among small-box states.
Exploration control: an entropy regularization term on the policy, with weight 0.1 (high) or 0.01 (low), sets the exploration rate.
Data: AI2-THOR scenes augmented with manually labeled object bounding boxes, plus a new turtle-bot conference-room dataset (27 locations x 8 views = 216 images).

setting.backbone: Frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features + FC recognition network (trained) + A3C-style actor-critic policy network (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: AI2-THOR (20 train / 10 val scenes) with manually annotated boxes for 4 objects in 4 scenes; 150 extra images per object for the real-world recognition module; RL trained on-policy in the discretized scenes
setting.observation: monocular RGB from the current view plus a target object image; no depth, map or odometry
setting.action_space: 8 discrete actions: MoveAhead/Back/Left/Right (fixed distance), LookUp/LookDown, RotateLeft/Right (90°); turtle-bot uses 6 actions
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (discretized scene graph of pre-captured images) plus a real discretized conference room
setting.privileged: Ground-truth bounding-box annotations used to train the recognition module; the goal threshold is defined from GT boxes. No map or pose at test time.

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 random-start episodes per target object; 5000-step cap
numbers.extra: Avg. len. counts successful episodes only
Real robot, discretized into 27 locations x 8 views

numbers_note: Only Table I and II report results. Avg. len. is over successful episodes only. Each cell uses about 10 episodes per object, so the numbers are noisy. The random-walk baseline in the 1-object scene is 2050.3 / 60.0%, and 820.9 / 99.0% on the turtle-bot.
results: The proposed reward with low exploration cuts average trajectory length from about 2050 (random walk) to 52.9 on 1 object/1 scene while reaching 100% success. Reward functions 1 and 2 fail to converge or do worse than random walk. High exploration gives higher success in multi-object/multi-scene settings (92.5%, 87.5%) but very long paths; on the real turtle-bot, both settings reach 100%, with 63.3 vs 176.8 average steps.
limitations: Tiny evaluation (10 episodes per object, discretized scenes, few scenes and objects), and the success rate is sensitive to the exploration rate; the low-exploration model gets trapped (fails on 'plate').
No memory unit and no commonsense or semantic priors; the policy is scene-specific and needs annotated boxes for the recognition module.
Reward functions 1 and 2 were not tested in multi-object/multi-scene settings due to compute limits, so the comparison there is partial.
compares_to: Reward function 1 (sparse goal reward, following Zhu et al.)
